title: Look into the back of a mask and your brain still sees a face bulging out

cover.alt: A computer-rendered mask seen from behind that still looks like a face bulging outwards, above a plain oval shell that looks hollow.

body: The inside of a face mask curves away from you, yet it looks like a normal, outward-bulging face. The psychologist Richard Gregory called this evidence for the power of **top-down knowledge** in vision: we have seen so many faces that bulge outwards that the brain’s bet overrides even the clear signal from our two eyes that the surface is hollow. A featureless hollow shape, lit and turned the same way, is seen correctly as hollow, which suggests that knowing what faces look like plays a big part.

slides.alt: A computer animation of two copper-coloured shapes turning on a black background: a face mask on top and a plain oval shell below. Even when the mask’s hollow back faces the viewer it looks like an outward face, while the plain shell looks hollow.
slides.caption: Both shapes spin all the way round. When the mask turns its hollow back to you, it still looks like a face bulging out; the plain shell below, lit the same way, looks hollow.
slides.credit: Iljsdf, Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · excerpt

slides.heading: What’s there vs what you see

left.label: What’s there
left.text: A concave mask, its nose the part farthest from you.

right.label: What you see
right.text: An ordinary face, its nose pointing straight at you.

steps.label: Light and shade reach your eyes
Both eyes signal that the face is hollow
Knowledge wins: you see a normal face

slides.prompt: In one experiment, people quickly flicked a finger at a small target attached inside a hollow face. Where did they aim?
slides.answer: At the real spot, not the one they saw
slides.detail: They still saw a normal face, yet their flicks went to the target’s true position. Fast cues steering the hand seem to be separate from the knowledge behind the illusion.

slides.heading: Not everyone is fooled as much
slides.text: The illusion is weaker in people with schizophrenia or other psychotic symptoms, and seems to strengthen in successfully treated patients. People on the autism spectrum have also been found less susceptible to visual illusions, this one included. Lighting a hollow face from below makes it stronger still.

slides.question: Which evidence does the hollow-face illusion manage to override?
slides.explanation: The brain’s strong expectation that faces bulge outwards beats even stereoscopic information from the two eyes signalling that the mask is hollow.
